title: Sleep and teenagers: seven short texts
texts: Many parents are puzzled when their teenage children seem wide awake at midnight and impossible to wake at seven. The explanation is partly biological. During adolescence, the internal body clock shifts, so that young people naturally feel sleepy later in the evening and wake later in the morning. This is not laziness, although it can look like it. It does, however, clash badly with school timetables that start early.

Doctors generally advise that people between thirteen and eighteen should sleep for about eight to ten hours a night. Few teenagers manage this. Surveys in many countries show that a large proportion get considerably less, particularly on school days. Some try to compensate at weekends, but sleeping until noon on Sunday only partly repairs the damage and may make it harder to fall asleep that night.

The light from phones, tablets and laptops contains a lot of blue wavelengths, which tell the brain that it is still daytime. As a result, the body produces less melatonin, the hormone that helps us feel sleepy. Experts therefore recommend putting screens away at least an hour before bed. Many devices now offer a warm-light mode, but researchers say that the content itself, which keeps the mind active, matters as well.

While we sleep, the brain is far from idle. It sorts the day's information, strengthens important connections and discards much of the rest. Students who study in the evening and then sleep well often remember more the next day than those who stay up revising all night. In other words, a night of sleep is not time lost from studying; it is part of the process of learning.

When tiredness strikes, many teenagers reach for an energy drink or a strong coffee. Caffeine reduces the feeling of tiredness, but it does not remove the need for sleep, and it stays in the body for many hours. A drink at four in the afternoon can still affect sleep at night, and the resulting tiredness the next day leads to another can. It is a cycle that is easy to start and hard to break.

Sleep specialists insist that the single most useful habit is not a gadget or a supplement but consistency. Going to bed and getting up at roughly the same time every day, including weekends, helps the body clock to settle. A cool, dark room and a calming routine, such as reading a paper book, also make it easier to switch off. Results usually appear within a couple of weeks.

A short nap can help, provided it is kept short. Around twenty or thirty minutes in the early afternoon is usually enough to improve alertness and mood without leaving a person groggy. Longer naps, or naps taken late in the day, may make it difficult to fall asleep in the evening. For students who have had a bad night, a brief rest is a practical emergency measure, but it cannot replace regular night sleep.
